name: Fadogia agrestis

track.title: Dietary supplement
track.line: Sold as a supplement; not reviewed by FDA

what.text: Fadogia agrestis (also classified as Vangueria agrestis) is a West African shrub. Its stem is used in traditional African medicine for pain, inflammation and as an aphrodisiac.
Products sold as dietary supplements claim to contain it. A 2019 lab analysis of 17 such supplements found the plant’s marker compounds in 12 and none in 5.
All published research on Fadogia agrestis and testosterone is in rats. No published human studies found as of November 1, 2026.

research.text: No published human studies found as of November 1, 2026. All the testosterone and sexual-function research is in rats, mostly from one research group in Nigeria.
Searches run on November 1, 2026 found no human study and no registered clinical trial of Fadogia agrestis.

research.title: Sexual behaviour and testosterone in male rats (Yakubu et al.)

facts.v: animal study; stem water extract given by mouth

research.found: Mating measures and blood testosterone rose in all dose groups. This is a rat study only.

src.label: Yakubu et al., Asian J Androl, 2005 (rats)

research.title: Testicular function in male rats over 28 days (Yakubu et al.)

facts.v: animal study with a 10-day recovery period
18, 50 or 100 mg/kg body weight a day
testis weight and testicular enzymes and chemistry

research.found: All doses changed testicular measures. The authors called these signs of adverse effects on testicular function; the rats recovered on some measures, mainly at the lowest dose.

research.title: Liver and kidney cell toxicity in male rats (Yakubu et al.)

facts.v: liver and kidney enzymes, serum markers of cell damage

research.found: The extract lowered enzyme activity in liver and kidney with matching rises in blood, and raised a marker of membrane damage (malondialdehyde). The authors suggest damage to liver and kidney cell membranes. No deaths or organ swelling were seen.

src.label: Yakubu et al., Hum Exp Toxicol, 2009 (rats)

research.text: A 2023 study in rats given paroxetine to cause erectile problems found the extract restored several penile and testicular chemical markers. This too is in rats only.

us.text: Fadogia agrestis is sold in the US as a dietary supplement. It is not an FDA-approved drug, and FDA does not review supplements for safety or effectiveness before sale. As of November 1, 2026.

items.text: Fadogia agrestis is a botanical. Under US law, a product meant to supplement the diet that contains an herb or other botanical can be sold as a dietary supplement.

src.label: 21 U.S.C. 321(ff), definition of dietary supplement, govinfo

items.text: FDA does not have the authority to approve dietary supplements before they are marketed, and a firm generally does not have to give FDA its safety evidence. FDA does not approve supplements or their labelling.

src.label: Questions and answers on dietary supplements, FDA

items.text: Fadogia agrestis is not an FDA-approved drug for any use, including low testosterone or erectile problems.

side.text: There is no human safety data. In rats, 28 days of the extract changed testicular measures and showed signs of liver and kidney cell damage.

items.text: the authors described adverse effects on testicular function at all doses, with partial recovery mainly at the lowest dose.
enzyme and membrane-damage markers suggested harm to liver and kidney cells.

items.text: 5 of 17 supplements labelled as Fadogia agrestis had none of the plant’s marker compounds.
FDA does not review dietary supplements for safety before they are sold, so product contents and strength are not checked by FDA.

surprises: Fadogia agrestis is sold to men for testosterone, but the main rat studies behind it also reported adverse effects on the testes and signs of liver and kidney cell damage.
